name: SMAS imbrication facelift

lead: In an SMAS imbrication facelift the surgeon tightens the superficial musculoaponeurotic system, the fibromuscular layer under facial skin, by overlapping and suturing it, then redrapes the skin. This lifts the cheeks, jowls and neck.
A randomized comparison of lifting vectors found oblique-vertical vectors gave better improvement of the malar eminence, melolabial fold and jowls.

paras: It is an operation by a surgeon, in the family of SMAS techniques that also includes plication, flaps and deep plane lifts.
Hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis and scarring are recognised; a meta-analysis found permanent nerve injury risk did not differ among techniques.

angle.text: Tightening the SMAS lifts sagging cheeks and jowls, with results that rely on deeper support rather than skin tension.

lead: The SMAS is a fibromuscular layer central to many facelifts; imbrication overlaps and sutures it to lift tissue.[1] Mitz and Peyronie described the SMAS in 1976.[1]
Related techniques include plication (folding and suturing), flap, and deep plane.[1] A 183-study meta-analysis compared complication rates across them.[2]
infobox: About 3-4 weeks for a traditional facelift

paras: Hematoma is the most common complication; nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and hairline changes can occur.[1] In the meta-analysis, high lateral SMAS and composite lifts had more temporary nerve injury than plication.[2]
A randomized comparison of 107 patients rated by three surgeons found oblique-vertical SMAS vectors improved malar eminence, melolabial fold and jowls better.[3]

timeline.event: Mitz and Peyronie describe the SMAS.[1]
